units.title: Open Loop vs Closed Loop
units.tip: A control system tells a device what to do. Open loop systems just issue commands without checking results. Closed loop systems measure the output and adjust the input to reach a goal.

exercises.question: What is an open loop control system?
exercises.answer: A system that sends commands without measuring or adjusting based on the output
exercises.explain: Open loop systems apply a fixed input and do not sense the result. A toaster set to 'medium' runs for a fixed time regardless of actual brownness.
choices: A system that has no physical parts
A system that continuously measures its output
A system that sends commands without measuring or adjusting based on the output
A system that only works with electrical signals

exercises.question: Which of these is an example of open loop control?
exercises.answer: A washing machine running through a fixed cycle time
exercises.explain: A washing machine runs for a set time regardless of how dirty the clothes are. It does not sense cleanliness and adjust.
choices: A thermostat adjusting heating based on room temperature
A water heater holding tank temperature constant
A washing machine running through a fixed cycle time
A cruise control maintaining a car's speed

exercises.question: What is a major disadvantage of open loop control?
exercises.answer: It cannot correct for disturbances or changes in the environment
exercises.explain: Without sensing feedback, an open loop system cannot detect or respond to unexpected changes, like wind affecting an airplane holding a heading.
choices: It is too expensive to build
It always makes the system unstable
It cannot correct for disturbances or changes in the environment
It requires a computer to operate

exercises.question: When can open loop control be a reasonable choice?
exercises.answer: Because the process is simple and predictable, so a fixed command reliably gives the wanted result
exercises.explain: If conditions are well known and disturbances are small, a fixed command is cheap and works well. A fixed-time toaster or sprinkler timer is a common case.
choices: Because feedback is never possible in any device
Because open loop systems cannot be disturbed
Because open loop is always more accurate than closed loop
Because the process is simple and predictable, so a fixed command reliably gives the wanted result

exercises.question: What does 'disturbance' mean in control theory?
exercises.answer: An unexpected change that affects the system output
exercises.explain: A disturbance is any external change: wind pushing an aircraft, a load added to a motor, or a door opened in a heated room.
choices: The feedback signal from a sensor
An unexpected change that affects the system output
A type of controller
The command input to the system

exercises.question: What is a closed loop control system?
exercises.answer: A system that measures output, compares it to a goal, and adjusts input to match the goal
exercises.explain: Closed loop systems use feedback. A thermostat measures room temperature, compares it to the setpoint, and turns heat on or off to match.
choices: A system that only uses mechanical parts
A system that runs at constant speed
A system that has no inputs or outputs
A system that measures output, compares it to a goal, and adjusts input to match the goal

exercises.question: Which of these is an example of closed loop control?
exercises.answer: A cruise control system adjusting engine power to maintain a constant speed
exercises.explain: Cruise control measures vehicle speed and adjusts throttle to keep speed constant even on hills or with changing air resistance.
choices: A cruise control system adjusting engine power to maintain a constant speed
A door opener that runs for a set time
A traffic light changing color at a fixed time
A car accelerating to 60 mph and staying there without any adjustments

exercises.question: What is the 'setpoint' or 'reference' in a closed loop system?
exercises.answer: The desired target value the system is trying to reach
exercises.explain: The setpoint is the goal: a thermostat's setpoint is the desired room temperature, and a cruise control's setpoint is the desired speed.
choices: The power supply voltage
The feedback sensor type
The desired target value the system is trying to reach
The actual measured value at any moment

exercises.question: What happens when the output differs from the setpoint?
exercises.answer: The system detects the error and changes the control input to reduce it
exercises.explain: If actual temperature is below setpoint, the system increases heat. If it is above, heat decreases. This is how feedback achieves goals.
choices: The system turns off immediately
The setpoint changes automatically
The sensor stops working
The system detects the error and changes the control input to reduce it

exercises.question: What is an advantage of closed loop control over open loop?
exercises.answer: It can automatically correct for disturbances and maintain accuracy
exercises.explain: Closed loop systems sense and adapt, so they handle unexpected changes. A thermostat holds temperature even if a window opens.
choices: It costs less to build
It does not need any sensors
It has no moving parts
It can automatically correct for disturbances and maintain accuracy

units.title: Feedback and Stability
units.tip: Feedback is the signal that tells a control system how close it is to the goal. Negative feedback reduces error and improves stability. Positive feedback makes changes grow and can cause instability.

exercises.question: What is negative feedback in control systems?
exercises.answer: Feedback that opposes the error and drives the system toward the setpoint
exercises.explain: Negative feedback reduces the difference between actual and desired values. A thermostat that heats when cold is using negative feedback: it opposes the temperature error.
choices: Feedback that makes errors larger
A signal that turns the system off
Feedback that opposes the error and drives the system toward the setpoint
A feedback signal that is always bad for the system

exercises.question: How does negative feedback improve system response?
exercises.answer: It reduces steady-state error and helps the system reach and hold the setpoint
exercises.explain: Negative feedback makes the system self-correcting. If the output drifts away from setpoint, feedback pushes it back.
choices: It makes the system response slower
It increases overshoot
It prevents any control action
It reduces steady-state error and helps the system reach and hold the setpoint

exercises.question: In a home heating system, how is negative feedback achieved?
exercises.answer: The thermostat senses temperature and turns heat on if too cold, off if too warm
exercises.explain: The temperature measurement is fed back and compared to setpoint. When actual is below setpoint, the error is positive, so heat turns on (negative feedback opposes the error).
choices: The thermostat ignores the actual temperature
The thermostat senses temperature and turns heat on if too cold, off if too warm
Heat intensity increases whenever the setpoint changes
The furnace always runs at maximum power

exercises.question: What is the 'error signal' in a feedback control system?
exercises.answer: The difference between the setpoint and the measured output
exercises.explain: Error = setpoint - actual output. A positive error means the output is too low; negative means too high.
choices: The difference between the setpoint and the measured output
The power supply current
A signal from a broken component
The sensor calibration value

exercises.question: Why is negative feedback called 'negative' if it improves the system?
exercises.answer: Because the feedback signal opposes (has the opposite sign to) the error
exercises.explain: If error is positive (too low), negative feedback means the control action increases the output. Negative refers to the mathematical relationship, not the quality.
choices: Because the feedback signal opposes (has the opposite sign to) the error
Because the feedback voltage is negative
Because it uses no electrical power
Because it always makes performance worse

exercises.question: What makes a control system stable?
exercises.answer: The output converges to the setpoint and stays there despite disturbances
exercises.explain: A stable system reaches its goal and holds it. An unstable system diverges and gets worse over time.
choices: The system has no feedback
The system never changes
The system is always at maximum output
The output converges to the setpoint and stays there despite disturbances

exercises.question: What is positive feedback?
exercises.answer: Feedback that reinforces the error and makes it grow
exercises.explain: Positive feedback amplifies changes. A microphone pointed at a speaker creates positive feedback: sound loops and grows louder (squealing).
choices: Feedback that is always good
Feedback that reinforces the error and makes it grow
The main control input
A signal that reduces error

exercises.question: Why does positive feedback usually make a system unstable?
exercises.answer: Because it amplifies errors instead of correcting them, causing the output to grow without bound
exercises.explain: With positive feedback, any small error gets magnified. The system diverges from setpoint rapidly and can become dangerous.
choices: Because it uses less power
Because it is slower than negative feedback
Because it requires no sensors
Because it amplifies errors instead of correcting them, causing the output to grow without bound

exercises.question: What is an example of positive feedback causing instability?
exercises.answer: An audio speaker feeding sound back into a microphone, causing oscillation and squealing
exercises.explain: Sound from the speaker re-enters the microphone, gets amplified, comes back out louder, and repeats. The system becomes unstable and audibly fails.
choices: A cruise control holding vehicle speed
A thermostat maintaining room temperature
An aircraft autopilot leveling the wings
An audio speaker feeding sound back into a microphone, causing oscillation and squealing

exercises.question: How does negative feedback prevent instability compared to positive feedback?
exercises.answer: Negative feedback opposes errors, driving the system back to setpoint, while positive feedback magnifies errors
exercises.explain: Negative feedback is self-correcting. Positive feedback is self-destabilizing. That is why most engineered systems use negative feedback.
choices: Positive feedback is more reliable
Negative feedback opposes errors, driving the system back to setpoint, while positive feedback magnifies errors
Negative feedback requires no measurements
Negative feedback uses more power

units.title: Block Diagrams and Transfer Functions
units.tip: Block diagrams visually show how signals flow in a control system. Transfer functions are mathematical descriptions of how a system responds to inputs. Both tools help engineers understand and design controllers.

exercises.question: What is a block diagram in control theory?
exercises.answer: A graphical representation showing how signals flow through a system
exercises.explain: Block diagrams use boxes (blocks) for components and arrows for signals. They show the overall structure and feedback loops without detailed math.
choices: A graphical representation showing how signals flow through a system
A wiring diagram for electronic circuits
A detailed list of all system parts
A time vs. output graph

exercises.question: What does a box (block) represent in a block diagram?
exercises.answer: A component or process that transforms an input signal into an output signal
exercises.explain: Each block represents a part of the system: a sensor, controller, motor, or plant. It shows the input-output relationship.
choices: A power supply
An error in the system
A component or process that transforms an input signal into an output signal
A feedback connection

exercises.question: What do arrows represent in a block diagram?
exercises.answer: Signal paths showing how information flows from one block to another
exercises.explain: Arrows carry signals (values like voltage, temperature, speed) from one component to the next.
choices: Power flow only
Signal paths showing how information flows from one block to another
Wires or physical connections only
Error signals only

exercises.question: In a closed loop block diagram, what happens at the summing junction?
exercises.answer: The reference signal and feedback signal are compared to compute the error
exercises.explain: A summing point (often shown as a circle with +/-) combines signals. In negative feedback, it computes error = setpoint - feedback.
choices: The reference signal and feedback signal are compared to compute the error
The controller is activated
The signal is split into two paths
The output is amplified

exercises.question: Why are block diagrams useful for understanding control systems?
exercises.answer: They show the overall structure and feedback paths without requiring detailed mathematics
exercises.explain: Block diagrams give a clear visual picture of how components interact and where feedback occurs, before diving into transfer functions.
choices: They guarantee stability automatically
They are required by law
They show the overall structure and feedback paths without requiring detailed mathematics
They eliminate the need for testing

exercises.question: What is a transfer function?
exercises.answer: A mathematical description of how a system's output responds to an input
exercises.explain: Transfer function G(s) relates output to input: output = G(s) * input. It captures the dynamics of a component in one equation.
choices: A wiring connection
A list of components in the system
The physical dimensions of a device
A mathematical description of how a system's output responds to an input

exercises.question: What does the notation G(s) mean in transfer function language?
exercises.answer: A transfer function in the Laplace domain, where s is the Laplace variable
exercises.explain: G(s) is shorthand for the input-output relationship in Laplace form. The variable s encodes frequency and time behavior.
choices: The speed of the system response
A transfer function in the Laplace domain, where s is the Laplace variable
A simple proportional relationship
The gain of the system multiplied by time

exercises.question: How does a higher transfer function gain affect the system response?
exercises.answer: A higher gain produces a larger output for the same input, making response faster but risking overshoot
exercises.explain: High gain amplifies the control signal, speeding up response but potentially causing oscillation. It is a tuning trade-off.
choices: It reduces the control effort
A higher gain produces a larger output for the same input, making response faster but risking overshoot
It has no effect on the response
It always makes the system more stable

exercises.question: What do poles of a transfer function determine?
exercises.answer: The natural frequencies and decay rates of the system response
exercises.explain: Poles in the left half-plane (negative real part) lead to stable decay. Poles on the right side cause divergence and instability.
choices: The power supply voltage
The input signal amplitude
The natural frequencies and decay rates of the system response
The sensor calibration

exercises.question: Why are transfer functions useful for control design?
exercises.answer: They allow engineers to analyze stability and predict response without building a prototype
exercises.explain: Transfer functions enable simulation and analysis. Engineers can check stability, overshoot, and speed mathematically before hardware testing.
choices: They eliminate all disturbances
They allow engineers to analyze stability and predict response without building a prototype
They guarantee perfect control
They reduce the cost of materials

units.title: Step Response Characteristics
units.tip: When you suddenly change the setpoint from 0 to 1, the system's response tells you how well it works. Rise time, overshoot, settling time, and steady-state error are key measures of performance.

exercises.question: What is 'rise time' in step response analysis?
exercises.answer: The time it takes for the output to go from 10 percent to 90 percent of the final value
exercises.explain: Rise time measures how fast the system reacts to a step input. Faster rise time means quicker response.
choices: The time the output overshoots
The time it takes for the output to go from 10 percent to 90 percent of the final value
The peak value the output reaches
The steady-state error of the system

exercises.question: What is 'overshoot' in a step response?
exercises.answer: The amount by which the output exceeds the setpoint before settling
exercises.explain: Overshoot happens when the system overshoots its target. A 20 percent overshoot means the peak is 120 percent of the desired value.
choices: The steady-state error
The final value of the output
The initial delay before the system responds
The amount by which the output exceeds the setpoint before settling

exercises.question: Why might a fast rise time come with large overshoot?
exercises.answer: High control effort needed for speed can push the output past the target
exercises.explain: To accelerate fast, the controller applies strong commands. By the time it realizes it has reached setpoint, inertia has carried it beyond.
choices: Fast systems never have feedback
High control effort needed for speed can push the output past the target
Overshoot and rise time are independent
Slow systems always overshoot

exercises.question: How is percent overshoot calculated?
exercises.answer: ((peak - final value) / final value) * 100 percent
exercises.explain: If the setpoint is 10 and the peak is 12, overshoot is (12-10)/10 * 100 = 20 percent.
choices: (peak / rise time)
((peak - final value) / final value) * 100 percent
(peak - final value) in units
(peak / final value) * 100 percent

exercises.question: In applications like aircraft autopilot, why is low overshoot important?
exercises.answer: Large overshoots can cause unsafe or uncomfortable maneuvers
exercises.explain: If an autopilot overshoots altitude by too much, it wastes fuel and discomforts passengers. Precision and smoothness matter.
choices: Overshoot does not affect real systems
Low overshoot means the system is broken
Aircraft always need maximum speed
Large overshoots can cause unsafe or uncomfortable maneuvers

exercises.question: What is 'settling time' in step response?
exercises.answer: The time it takes for the output to settle within a tolerance band around the final value
exercises.explain: Settling time is typically defined as reaching and staying within 2 percent of the final value. It includes all oscillations and decay.
choices: The initial rise time
The time it takes for the output to settle within a tolerance band around the final value
The steady-state value itself
The peak of the overshoot

exercises.question: What is 'steady-state error'?
exercises.answer: The persistent difference between the setpoint and the final output value
exercises.explain: Steady-state error is the error that remains after the system settles. A good controller minimizes this.
choices: The overshoot of the system
The time to reach setpoint
The noise in the measurement
The persistent difference between the setpoint and the final output value

exercises.question: How does a longer settling time affect system performance?
exercises.answer: It means the system takes longer to stabilize, which is undesirable in most applications
exercises.explain: Long settling times mean the system oscillates or drifts for a long time before settling. Faster settling is better.
choices: It improves stability
It guarantees zero overshoot
It reduces steady-state error
It means the system takes longer to stabilize, which is undesirable in most applications

exercises.question: Why is steady-state error important to minimize in a temperature control system?
exercises.answer: To ensure the actual temperature closely matches the desired setpoint value
exercises.explain: If there is steady-state error, the oven is always a few degrees off setpoint, wasting energy and possibly damaging products.
choices: To eliminate all disturbances
To ensure the actual temperature closely matches the desired setpoint value
To reduce the cost of the sensor
To speed up the rise time

exercises.question: What is a common trade-off when tuning a system to reduce overshoot?
exercises.answer: Reducing overshoot by lowering the gain usually makes the rise slower
exercises.explain: Lowering the gain cuts overshoot but slows the response. Raising the gain speeds the response but risks overshoot. Engineers balance these.
choices: Steady-state error always increases when overshoot decreases
There is no trade-off, overshoot and speed can both be minimized freely
Rise time is independent of control gain
Reducing overshoot by lowering the gain usually makes the rise slower

units.title: PID Control
units.tip: PID stands for Proportional, Integral, Derivative. Each term handles a different aspect of error. Proportional responds to current error, Integral eliminates steady-state error, and Derivative predicts and damps overshoot.

exercises.question: What does the Proportional term do in a PID controller?
exercises.answer: It produces a control effort proportional to the current error
exercises.explain: P term = Kp * error. The larger the error, the stronger the response. It provides immediate correction.
choices: It prevents overshoot entirely
It eliminates all steady-state error
It produces a control effort proportional to the current error
It increases the system gain infinitely

exercises.question: What does the Integral term do in a PID controller?
exercises.answer: It accumulates error over time and eliminates steady-state error
exercises.explain: I term integrates error, building up control effort as long as error persists. This forces the output to match setpoint exactly over time.
choices: It makes the response slower
It increases overshoot
It responds only to high-frequency noise
It accumulates error over time and eliminates steady-state error

exercises.question: What does the Derivative term do in a PID controller?
exercises.answer: It responds to the rate of change of error, damping overshoot and oscillation
exercises.explain: D term = Kd * (de/dt). If error is decreasing fast, D reduces control effort to prevent overshooting. It anticipates the future.
choices: It adds noise to the system
It responds to the rate of change of error, damping overshoot and oscillation
It has no effect on transient response
It accelerates the response

exercises.question: Which PID term is most sensitive to measurement noise?
exercises.answer: The Derivative term, because it amplifies noise in the error signal
exercises.explain: D term takes the time derivative of error. Noise has very fast changes, so high-frequency noise gets greatly amplified by the derivative.
choices: The Integral term
All three are equally sensitive
The Proportional term
The Derivative term, because it amplifies noise in the error signal

exercises.question: What is the complete PID control law?
exercises.answer: Control = Kp * error + Ki * integral(error) + Kd * derivative(error)
exercises.explain: The PID controller sums the three terms: proportional (current error), integral (accumulated error), and derivative (rate of error change).
choices: Control = Kp * error + Ki * integral(error) + Kd * derivative(error)
Control = Kp + Ki + Kd
Control = error / (Kp * Ki * Kd)
Control = Kp * Ki * Kd * error

exercises.question: What is the effect of increasing the Proportional gain Kp?
exercises.answer: Faster response, but higher overshoot and risk of instability if too high
exercises.explain: High Kp makes the system react more aggressively. Response speeds up but becomes less stable if Kp exceeds a limit.
choices: No change to the response
Elimination of all overshoot
Faster response, but higher overshoot and risk of instability if too high
Slower response and increased steady-state error

exercises.question: What happens if the Integral gain Ki is too high?
exercises.answer: Steady-state error is eliminated but the system becomes very prone to overshoot and oscillation
exercises.explain: High Ki accumulates error quickly, pushing hard to eliminate offset. This causes the output to overshoot and ring.
choices: Measurement noise is eliminated
Steady-state error is eliminated but the system becomes very prone to overshoot and oscillation
The system response becomes very slow
The Proportional term is cancelled

exercises.question: How does increasing Derivative gain Kd affect the response?
exercises.answer: It damps overshoot and reduces oscillation, making the response smoother
exercises.explain: Higher Kd means the controller more aggressively brakes as error decreases, preventing overshoot and smoothing transients.
choices: It makes noise dominate the control signal
It eliminates steady-state error
It damps overshoot and reduces oscillation, making the response smoother
It increases overshoot

exercises.question: In a system with significant measurement noise, which PID term should be de-emphasized?
exercises.answer: The Derivative term, because it amplifies high-frequency noise
exercises.explain: If sensors are noisy, a high Kd will make the noisy signal changes drive wild control swings. Use moderate Kd in noisy systems.
choices: All terms must be equal strength
The Integral term
The Proportional term
The Derivative term, because it amplifies high-frequency noise

exercises.question: Why is a pure P controller often inadequate for temperature control?
exercises.answer: It cannot eliminate steady-state error, so the system settles at a temperature offset from setpoint
exercises.explain: P controller requires error to generate output. At steady state with zero error, P produces zero output, so it cannot hold setpoint if there is any heat loss.
choices: It makes the system too fast
It requires no tuning
It cannot eliminate steady-state error, so the system settles at a temperature offset from setpoint
It causes infinite oscillation

units.title: Tuning and Real-World Applications
units.tip: PID tuning is the art of choosing Kp, Ki, and Kd to achieve good performance. Different applications need different trade-offs. Real systems have constraints, nonlinearities, and delays that affect how well theory works in practice.

exercises.question: What is the Ziegler-Nichols tuning method?
exercises.answer: A classic method: increase P gain until oscillation, then calculate Kp, Ki, and Kd from that critical point
exercises.explain: Ziegler-Nichols finds the critical gain where the system oscillates at the edge of stability, then scales back to a reasonable operating point.
choices: A method that requires simulation only
A procedure that guarantees perfect response
A tuning method that sets all gains to zero
A classic method: increase P gain until oscillation, then calculate Kp, Ki, and Kd from that critical point

exercises.question: Why is manual tuning sometimes preferred over automated methods?
exercises.answer: It allows engineers to account for application-specific priorities and constraints not captured by algorithms
exercises.explain: An engineer might accept more overshoot for a faster response, or add damping to limit noise sensitivity. Automated methods only optimize the goals they are given, so they may miss application-specific priorities.
choices: Manual tuning is always faster
It allows engineers to account for application-specific priorities and constraints not captured by algorithms
Automated methods cannot be implemented in practice
Automated methods are always unstable

exercises.question: What is 'gain scheduling' in control design?
exercises.answer: Automatically changing controller gains based on operating conditions or setpoint changes
exercises.explain: Gain scheduling adjusts Kp, Ki, and Kd as the system changes. For example, a cruise control might use different gains at highway speed vs. slow city speed.
choices: Eliminating feedback entirely
Using only the Proportional term
Tuning the controller once and never changing it
Automatically changing controller gains based on operating conditions or setpoint changes

exercises.question: What is 'model predictive control' (MPC)?
exercises.answer: A method that predicts future system behavior and optimizes control inputs over a time horizon
exercises.explain: MPC uses a model of the system to forecast what will happen. It chooses control inputs that minimize a cost function into the future.
choices: A control method that requires no computation
The same as PID control
A method that predicts future system behavior and optimizes control inputs over a time horizon
A method that does not use feedback

exercises.question: Why is 'anti-windup' important in integral control?
exercises.answer: To prevent the integral term from growing unboundedly when the system is saturated or cannot respond
exercises.explain: If the actual output is clamped by a limit (like max power), the integral keeps accumulating error. Anti-windup stops integration when saturation occurs.
choices: To prevent the integral term from growing unboundedly when the system is saturated or cannot respond
To reduce the effect of measurement noise
To speed up the Derivative term
To eliminate the Proportional term

exercises.question: In a robot arm position control, what is a key design trade-off?
exercises.answer: Speed of movement vs. precision and smoothness of motion
exercises.explain: Fast movement requires high gains and aggressive control, which can cause jerky motion and oscillation. Smooth motion needs lower gains and lower speed.
choices: Cost vs. reliability only
Motor size vs. system weight only
Using feedback vs. not using feedback
Speed of movement vs. precision and smoothness of motion

exercises.question: In aircraft altitude hold, why is a low overshoot essential?
exercises.answer: Large altitude overshoots waste fuel and discomfort passengers
exercises.explain: Overshooting altitude means the plane climbs too high, then dives to correct. This costs fuel and passenger comfort matters.
choices: Large altitude overshoots waste fuel and discomfort passengers
Overshoot always makes the plane faster
The autopilot is not used in aircraft
Altitude is not important in flight

exercises.question: What does 'time delay' or 'dead time' in a system mean?
exercises.answer: A lag between applying a control input and observing the effect on the output
exercises.explain: Dead time makes control harder. By the time the system reacts, the controller has already sent new commands. Excessive dead time causes instability.
choices: A permanent offset in the setpoint
The time the system is turned off
A lag between applying a control input and observing the effect on the output
A measure of the sensor accuracy

exercises.question: How does dead time affect PID tuning?
exercises.answer: Dead time makes the system harder to control, requiring more conservative (lower) gains to maintain stability
exercises.explain: With dead time, the system response is delayed relative to commands. High gains cause the controller to overcorrect. Dead time limits how fast safe control can be.
choices: Dead time always improves stability
Dead time eliminates the need for feedback
Dead time has no effect on tuning
Dead time makes the system harder to control, requiring more conservative (lower) gains to maintain stability

exercises.question: In an industrial oven, why might the I term be tuned more aggressively than in an aircraft?
exercises.answer: Oven temperature regulation does not require smoothness, only accuracy, so eliminating steady-state error is the priority
exercises.explain: A slow rise in temperature to setpoint is acceptable for baking. The goal is correct final temperature, not smooth motion. Aircraft prioritize smooth, predictable response.
choices: Industrial controllers are always better
Temperature control never uses integral terms
Oven temperature regulation does not require smoothness, only accuracy, so eliminating steady-state error is the priority
Ovens are always simpler than aircraft
